title: Redis
subtitle: Single-threaded event loop mechanics, core data structures, RDB vs AOF durability, and Cluster hash slot distribution.
keyTakeaways: Redis achieves 100,000+ operations/sec on a single core using an event loop with non-blocking I/O multiplexing (`epoll`), eliminating mutex lock contention.
Selecting the correct data structure matters: Sorted Sets (`ZSET`) back leaderboards and rate limiters; Hashes reduce memory overhead via ziplist encoding.
Redis Cluster partitions keys across 16,384 fixed hash slots (`CRC16(key) % 16384`) without a centralized proxy; multi-key operations require `{hash_tag}` braces.
architectureDiagram:
REDIS ARCHITECTURE: EVENT LOOP & CLUSTER HASH SLOTS

                                                    |

  +------------------------+  +------------------------+  +------------------------+

sections.heading: Data Structures and the Single-Threaded Event Loop
sections.body: Because Redis executes commands sequentially on a single thread in memory, every command and embedded Lua script runs atomically without mutexes. However, this architectural choice means long-running O(N) commands like `KEYS *`, `SMEMBERS` on a 1-million-item set, or slow Lua scripts freeze the entire Redis server, triggering cascading timeouts across upstream services.
bullets: Strings & Hashes: Hashes store objects with less memory than JSON strings because small hashes are encoded internally as compact contiguous memory buffers (ziplists).
Sorted Sets (`ZSET`): Backed by a Hash Table (O(1) member lookups) and a Skip List (O(log N) rank and score range queries). Essential for leaderboards and sliding-window rate limiters.
HyperLogLog (`PFADD`, `PFCOUNT`): Estimates unique cardinality (e.g., unique daily website visitors) with 0.81% standard error using a fixed 12 KB of memory, even for 100 million distinct elements.
Pipelining: Batches multiple commands into a single TCP socket write, eliminating round-trip latency overhead.

sections.heading: Persistence Trade-Offs and Cluster Architecture
sections.body: When used for stateful workloads like sessions or leaderboards, Redis provides two distinct persistence mechanisms alongside its horizontal sharding architecture.
bullets: RDB Snapshots (`BGSAVE`): Uses OS `fork()` and Copy-on-Write (CoW) memory pages to dump a point-in-time binary snapshot to disk. Extremely fast restarts, but loses minutes of data between snapshot intervals.

Append-Only File (AOF): Appends every write command sequentially (`appendfsync everysec`). Limits data loss to at most 1 second with minimal performance overhead. Redis 7+ combines an RDB base snapshot with incremental AOF logs.

Redis Cluster (16,384 Slots): Smart clients compute `CRC16(key) & 16383` and connect directly to the owning master node. If slots are migrating, nodes return `-MOVED` or `-ASK` redirects. Use `{hash_tag}` braces (`{user:101}:profile`) to force related keys onto the same slot for multi-key transactions.

tradeOffs.pros: Compact single-file backups; fast server reboot times; minimal disk I/O overhead during normal operations.
tradeOffs.cons: Loses all writes since the last snapshot on sudden power failure; `fork()` can double memory usage on write-heavy nodes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Pure caches where data can be reconstructed from primary databases.

tradeOffs.pros: Limits potential data loss to at most 1 second; append-only format avoids corruption.
tradeOffs.cons: Larger disk footprint; background log rewrites (`BGREWRITEAOF`) consume disk I/O.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time leaderboards, session stores, rate limiting buckets, and message queues.

interviewTip: Never say `KEYS *` in a system design interview. Always state: 'Because Redis is single-threaded, `KEYS *` blocks the server until full traversal completes. In production, we must use `SCAN` with cursor-based iteration to scan keys incrementally without blocking the event loop.'
